children: What are the most attractive Big Pharma stocks right now for investors?
Seeking Alpha analysts
and
gave us their picks.
Stephen Ayers: When it comes to Big Pharma stocks, I'm still interested in obesity names like Eli Lilly
and Novo Nordisk

. Both companies recently delivered solid Q3 earnings beats, and I think the obesity market is still early. And it's not so much about obesity itself, but the amount of cash these companies will be able to invest in other R&D efforts from obesity treatment revenues, like AI in drug development.
A couple of “up-and-coming” Big Pharma names I'm also watching in this space include Amgen
, which is preparing to launch a monthly GLP-1 agonist/GIP antagonist, and Roche

, whose acquisition of Carmot Therapeutics bolstered its obesity treatment pipeline. These two companies aren't as concentrated in just one therapeutic area, like Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, and they are also more likely to advance "under the radar."
Edmund Ingham: If I had to select three pharmas to invest in today, I would select Eli Lilly
, Roche
, and Merck
I'd select Eli Lilly

because, despite its all-time high share price and valuation that has surged past the trillion-dollar mark, a first for a pharma company, Lilly is the dominant player in the emerging GLP-1 peptide anti-obesity market, which could become the biggest pharma market of all time.
With Lilly

, we are entering uncharted territory. It is difficult to put a ceiling on how much revenue the company may generate from its market-leading approved molecule, tirzepatide, and its even more impressive-looking (in terms of mean weight loss, >28% at 80 weeks) clinical-stage candidate, retatrutide. Many observers thought a $1T dollar market cap for a pharma company was unobtainable, but I am now beginning to wonder if $2T is the next milestone Lilly will tick off. The company just hiked its full-year 2026 guidance by a staggering >$5B.
I'd select Roche

because it is, in my view, the most balanced global pharma, with exceptional strength in oncology, neuroscience, hematology, immunology, and ophthalmology. It also has a promising obesity/GLP-1 pipeline that could break up the Eli Lilly/Novo Nordisk
duopoly. Roche's thriving diagnostics division adds further diversity and ~$20B of additional annual revenues to the equation.
I'd pick Merck

because while the market frets about the impending patent expiry of its >$30B cancer drug Keytruda (pembrolizumab), it has quietly compiled, organically and inorganically, the most impressive oncology pipeline of any pharma, even Roche. Therefore, while a “trough year” (revenues falling year-on-year) may occur around 2028 when generic Keytruda is expected to flood the market, I suspect the company is better prepared to return to strong growth than the Street believes.
ALLKA Research: The VanEck Biotech ETF
and iShares Biotechnology ETF
are trading at multi-year highs. This is understandable given that Big Pharma players, including Gilead Sciences
, Merck
, and Eli Lilly
, beat consensus estimates by a wide margin.

In particular, as I noted in my recent article on Gilead, my favorite in the HIV market, the company's revenue rose 6.8% year-over-year to $8.3B in Q3. In my view, the key growth drivers were Biktarvy, Yeztugo, and Livdelzi, whose total sales were $4.57B, up 19.2% year-over-year.
Meanwhile, I believe Sanofi
, one of the leaders in the IMIDs treatment market, remains an undervalued Big Pharma player. Its flagship drug, Dupixent, developed in partnership with Regeneron
, generated €5.69B in Q3, up 35% year-over-year.
